about: Lines shown under the day in the Case Log app. quotes: c = when (or = days with cases, clinic = weekdays with no cases, off = weekends, empty = any day with no cases, any = every day). facts: one-line spine facts shown under the quote on days with no cases; src = short citation. Added to monthly.

facts.t: About two-thirds of lumbar disc herniations regress without surgery, and sequestered fragments resorb most often.
Adjacent-segment disease after cervical fusion appears at about 2.9% per year, roughly a quarter of patients by 10 years.
Disc bulges show up on MRI in 30% of pain-free 20-year-olds and 84% of pain-free 80-year-olds.
About a third of people with no back pain have a substantial abnormality on lumbar MRI.
C5 palsy follows cervical decompression in roughly 1 in 20 cases, and most recover.
Decompression within 48 hours of cauda equina syndrome is linked to better bladder and motor outcomes.
In SPORT, patients treated surgically for lumbar disc herniation improved more than nonoperative patients in the as-treated analysis.
In SPORT’s stenosis cohort, surgery gave greater improvement in pain and function at 2 years in the as-treated analysis.
A pelvic incidence to lumbar lordosis mismatch under 10 degrees is a core adult deformity target.
In adults the spinal cord usually ends at the L1-L2 level.
The vertebral artery enters the transverse foramen at C6 in about 90% of people.
There are 8 cervical nerve roots but only 7 cervical vertebrae; C8 exits below C7.
Odontoid fractures are the most common cervical spine fracture in patients over 70.
Vertebral compression fractures are the most common osteoporotic fracture.
OPLL affects roughly 2% to 4% of adults in Japan, far more than in Western populations.
Raymond Roy-Camille began placing pedicle screws with plates in France in 1963.
Paul Harrington developed his rod in Houston in the 1950s, first for scoliosis in polio survivors.
Smith and Robinson described the anterior cervical approach in 1955. Cloward published his dowel technique in 1958.
Mixter and Barr linked the ruptured disc to sciatica in 1934, launching lumbar disc surgery.
Yasargil and Caspar each introduced the operating microscope to lumbar discectomy in 1977.
Hibbs and Albee both reported the first spinal fusions in 1911, originally for spinal tuberculosis.
Victor Horsley performed the first successful removal of a spinal cord tumor by laminectomy in 1887.
Cotrel-Dubousset instrumentation arrived in 1984 and brought segmental rod-and-hook correction to scoliosis.
Galibert and Deramond performed the first vertebroplasty in France in 1984, for a C2 hemangioma.
Kyphoplasty balloons were cleared by the FDA in 1998.
The Charité disc was designed in East Berlin in the 1980s and became the first FDA-approved lumbar disc replacement in 2004.
The Prestige ST became the first FDA-approved cervical disc replacement in 2007.
The halo vest was introduced in 1959 at Rancho Los Amigos by Perry and Nickel, originally for polio patients.
Gardner-Wells tongs date to 1973 and replaced earlier skull calipers that needed drilling.
Percivall Pott described tuberculous spondylitis in 1779. It still carries his name.
Jean Lhermitte described the electric shock down the spine with neck flexion in 1924.
Spurling and Scoville described the foraminal compression test in 1944.
Brown-Séquard described hemisection of the cord in 1850.
Holger Scheuermann, a Danish radiologist, described his juvenile kyphosis in 1920.
G.Q. Chance described the horizontal flexion-distraction fracture of the lumbar spine in 1948.
Geoffrey Jefferson described the burst fracture of the atlas in 1920.
Schneider coined “hangman’s fracture” in 1965, comparing C2 pars fractures to judicial hanging injuries.
Mario Bertolotti described back pain from a lumbosacral transitional vertebra in 1917.
Oscar Batson showed in 1940 that the valveless vertebral venous plexus carries metastases to the spine.
Albert Adamkiewicz described the great anterior radiculomedullary artery in 1882.
Meyerding published his spondylolisthesis grading system in 1932.
Francis Denis proposed the three-column model of thoracolumbar fractures in 1983.
Gordon Waddell published his nonorganic signs of low back pain in 1980.
The Oswestry Disability Index was published in 1980 and is still the most used lumbar outcome score.
The atlas is named for the Titan who held up the heavens, since C1 holds up the head.
The axis gets its name because the head rotates around the dens.
“Vertebra” comes from the Latin vertere, to turn.
“Sacrum” comes from os sacrum, the “sacred bone.”
“Spondylolisthesis” is Greek for a slipping vertebra: spondylos plus olisthesis.
“Coccyx” comes from the Greek for cuckoo, after its resemblance to a cuckoo’s beak.
“Cauda equina” is Latin for horse’s tail.
The ligamentum flavum is yellow because it is rich in elastin.
“Lamina” is Latin for a thin plate.
Quiz: Which vertebra has no body? The atlas, C1.
Quiz: Which cervical vertebra has the most prominent spinous process? C7, the vertebra prominens.
Quiz: A paracentral L4-5 herniation usually hits which root? L5.
Quiz: A far lateral L4-5 herniation usually hits which root? L4.
Quiz: Weak deltoid points to which root? C5.
Quiz: A lost triceps reflex points to which root? C7.
Quiz: Weak big toe extension points to which root? L5, through extensor hallucis longus.
Quiz: A lost ankle jerk points to which root? S1.
Quiz: Numbness over the medial malleolus points to which root? L4.
Quiz: Which artery supplies the anterior two thirds of the cord? The anterior spinal artery.
Quiz: Which ligament lines the back of the vertebral bodies inside the canal? The PLL.
Cervical roots exit above their same-numbered vertebra. From T1 down, roots exit below.
Uncovertebral joints, the joints of Luschka, exist only from C3 to C7.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch, giving it a more predictable course for a left ACDF approach.
The artery of Adamkiewicz arises on the left in most people, usually between T9 and T12.
Lumbar facets face mostly sagittal, which resists rotation. Thoracic facets face mostly coronal.
The sinuvertebral nerve supplies the outer annulus and the PLL.
An atlantodens interval over 3 mm in an adult suggests transverse ligament insufficiency.
The multifidus is the most medial lumbar paraspinal muscle and is often atrophied in chronic low back pain.
The thoracic cord has its thinnest blood supply around T4 to T9, the classic watershed zone.
Low back pain is the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide.
Up to 84% of adults will have low back pain at some point in life.
Most acute low back pain improves substantially within the first 6 weeks.
Pars defects are found in about 4% of 6-year-olds and about 6% of adults.
Most spondylolysis occurs at L5.
Degenerative spondylolisthesis is most common at L4-5 and several times more common in women.
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis of 10 degrees or more affects about 2% to 3% of adolescents.
Only about one third of osteoporotic vertebral fractures come to clinical attention.
facts.src: Cooper et al., J Bone Miner Res 1992

facts.t: About 1 in 5 women with a new vertebral fracture has another within a year.
Cervical radiculopathy strikes about 83 per 100,000 people a year, and C7 is the root most often involved.
About 95% of lumbar disc herniations occur at L4-5 or L5-S1.
Degenerative cervical myelopathy is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults.
The US sees roughly 18,000 new spinal cord injuries a year.
Vehicle crashes are the leading cause of spinal cord injury in the US, with falls close behind.
